2. Brief facts as per DAR are that on 24.06.2018, deceased Harvinder Madan alongwith his wife Bharti Madan and friends/acquaintances namely Satyaranjan and Gurvinder Singh were travelling in an Etios Toyota Car bearing registration no. DL 8C AB 3910, owned and driven by deceased.

At about 01:30 am they reached on Elevated Road, Outer Ring Road, West Enclave, Mangolpuri, Delhi,
the car was collided with a truck bearing registration no. RJ 14 GD 4537 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle), which was abandoned/stationed on the road without any hazard warning lights or reflectors.
Information regarding the accident was lodged in PS Mangolpuri vide DD no. 3A.
Three occupants of car were declared brought dead in hospital and one expired during treatment.

sentences.text: It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and

Accident is not disputed by any respondents.
However, it is claim of R3 that offending vehicle was broke down and deceased hit the offending vehicle from behind.
Therefore, accident occurred due to sole negligence of deceased.
Hence, if not wholly, deceased was also contributory negligent.
16. Record shows that the car hit the truck from behind which was stationed on the road.

However,
the claim of R3 that the offeniding vehicle was stationed on the road as it was out of order holds no water because from the mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle, it is clear that offending vehicle was fit for road test.

Moreover petitioner has examined Pw2 who deposed that before the accident, he asked the R1 to remove the offending vehicle or to put hazard warning lights alerting the other vehicles passing from there.
Parking a vehicle on the on the road, particularly in pitch- dark conditions without indicators, is prima facie a negligence of its driver.
17. It is also the claim of R3 that deceased was driving the car at such a high speed that after hitting the offending vehicle from behind all four occupants of the car got expired.
It is also stated that if the car was at a permissible or moderate speed at the time of accident, the accident could be averted.

However, it is unreasonable to expect a driver to detect an unlit, stationary object on a dark highway, even at moderate MACT Case No. 501/2019 (FIR no. 542/2018) MACT Case No. 249/2019 (FIR no. 542/2018) Sanchita Madan Vs. Mubarak Shah & Ors.

sentences.text: It is also contended by R3 that the flyover where the accident occurred is vide enough to allow passing of three vehicles at a time and the truck being stationed at the extreme left side of the road

,
R1 cannot be held solely negligent.
The site plan shows that the place of accident is the depression of flyover where there is an exit from the flyover.
The truck was stationed immediately before exit.
It is submitted for the petitioners that to go to the residence of one of the occupant, one has to take very exit from the flyover.
Therefore, the car driver must be driving to the left side of the road.
As the hazards lights were not on and the car driver had no occassion to assume that truck is not moving.
A thought of stopping or slowing would never have come to the mind of driver.
Once the car reached near the truck, it was too late to stop and the car came under the rear of the truck.

19. In view of the facts disclose in the claim petition which proves place of incident as well as caused of death and on the basis of aforesaid discussion and the evidence which has come on record, it is held that the negligence on the part of driver of the offending vehicle was responsible not only for this accident, but also for everything that followed thereafter and there was no contributory negligence of deceased driver.
Accordingly issue no.1 is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and
also in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
& Ors., MACT Case No. 501/2019 (FIR no. 542/2018) MACT Case No. 249/2019 (FIR no.
542/2018) Sanchita Madan Vs. Mubarak Shah & Ors.

Therefore, accident occurred due to sole negligence of deceased.
Hence, if not wholly, deceased was also contributory negligent.
However,
the claim of R3 that the offeniding vehicle was stationed on the road as it was out of order holds no water because from the mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle, it is clear that offending vehicle was fit for road test.
Parking a vehicle on the on the road, particularly in pitch- dark conditions without indicators, is prima facie a negligence of its driver.
However, it is unreasonable to expect a driver to detect an unlit, stationary object on a dark highway, even at moderate MACT Case No. 501/2019 (FIR no. 542/2018) MACT Case No. 249/2019 (FIR no. 542/2018) Sanchita Madan Vs. Mubarak Shah & Ors.
Basically only three facts need to be established by the claimants for assessing compensation in the case of death : (a) age of the deceased; (b) income of the deceased; and the (c) the number of dependents.
The issues to be determined by the Tribunal to arrive at the loss of dependency are (i)
additions/deductions to be made for arriving at the income;
(ii) the deduction to be made towards the personal living expenses of the deceased; and (iii) the multiplier to be applied with reference of the age of the deceased.
Hence, the multiplier of "9" would be applicable in view of pronouncement made in case titled as Sarla Verma (supra).
